content.p: In the years after 2005, a man on Italy's list of its thirty most dangerous fugitives lived in a lakeside condominium outside Toronto, with drivers for his Range Rover, Porsche Cayenne and Ferrari. Giuseppe Coluccio, the eldest of three brothers from a 'Ndrangheta family on Calabria's Ionian coast, had left Italy in 2005, as Italian drug charges closed in. On 7 August 2008 he was arrested at a strip mall in Markham, Ontario, and thirteen days later he was on a plane to Rome.

Italian investigators describe him as a leading figure in cocaine and heroin trafficking between Latin America and Europe. He was not tried in Canada. Canada removed him on immigration grounds, and the Italian courts took over. The wider story, drawn from Italian investigations and Canadian press reporting, also takes in his brothers Salvatore and Antonio and the Ontario underworld they moved in.
content.h2: A clan built on a murdered father
content.p: The National Post named Giuseppe, Salvatore and Antonio Coluccio as the three sons of Vincenzo Coluccio, a mafia boss murdered in 1971 amid a mob feud in Gioiosa Jonica, the family's hometown. Authorities say the sons took the family's leadership as part of an alliance of three clans that grew into the strongest criminal group in Italy's south. An analyst whose article appears on Gangsters Inc. gives the brothers' birth years as 1966 (Giuseppe), 1967 (Salvatore) and 1969 (Antonio), and calls Giuseppe the first-born and most authoritative of them.

Italian investigators say the family's main business was international drug trafficking. In their account, as reported by France 24, Giuseppe had been a leading figure on the international drug scene since the early 1990s as head of one of the 'Ndrangheta clans. France 24 added that he was accused of having organised a network with a Turkish criminal organisation that carried narcotics towards the Calabrian coast on fishing boats belonging to the 'Ndrangheta. Corriere della Sera said he was accused of mafia association, of association aimed at drug trafficking, and of extortion.

Corriere reported that he had been wanted since 2005, when he escaped arrest in Operation Nostromo, coordinated by the anti-mafia prosecutors of Reggio Calabria. A source quoted by the analyst at Cosa Nostra News dates the Italian arrest warrant to June 2005. The National Post reported that the three brothers reached Ontario in 2005, shortly before serious drug charges in Italy were brought against Salvatore and Giuseppe. Antonio, who faced no charges, settled openly in Richmond Hill with his Canadian wife.

OCCRP reported that the Italian authorities convicted him in his absence on drugs, weapons and conspiracy charges after he disappeared in 2005, and that the prosecution alleged he belonged to a 'Ndrangheta group controlling maritime drug traffic along a 40-mile stretch of the southern Italian coast. France 24, by contrast, wrote on the day of his return that he was "accused" of drug trafficking, extortion and mafia association. The two outlets described his legal position differently.

OCCRP said he had lived in Canada for only a few years under an assumed name and was living a luxurious life outside Toronto, his days filled with meetings in clubs and cafés, OCCRP wrote, with men police have named as the top tier of organised crime in Ontario. Police began monitoring him and his fugitive brother Salvatore in 2006, according to the same report.

The National Post wrote that in Toronto's underworld the arrival of the Coluccios made waves: given their family name and contacts, the established Ontario 'Ndrangheta leaders found room for them at the table, perhaps even at its head. Giuseppe lived in a luxury waterfront condominium under a false name, while Salvatore soon vanished again.

Italian police also reported a link to Sicilian traffickers. According to Corriere, investigators of the Carabinieri's ROS unit said that while living under a false identity Giuseppe kept constant contact with Calabria, managing shipments of large quantities of hashish and cocaine for the clans of the Ionian coast around Reggio, and that in Canada he came into close contact with Giuseppe Cuntrera, known as "Big Joe", a member of the Sicilian Caruana-Cuntrera drug-trafficking family. Corriere said the two were business partners in a Toronto food company called Mangiare and that frequent meetings between them in public places in Ontario had been documented. The Cosa Nostra News author, who describes Cuntrera as a Woodbridge resident, repeats the Mangiare partnership and says that Cuntrera and Coluccio met several times.

Canadian authorities arrested him on immigration charges on 7 August 2008, in the suburb of Markham. OCCRP reported that he made no challenge at his immigration hearing to the finding that he could not stay, which rested on a drug conviction from 1993. Canadian officials held that his alleged organised-crime ties made him a danger, and he stayed in custody until he was deported.

Corriere reported that the arrest was made by ROS carabinieri together with Canadian police, three years into the search, and that he was found with about 1.5 million Canadian dollars in cash, traveller's cheques, cheques and jewels. It added that the Canadian authorities had refused bail in the days after the arrest. France 24 cited an Italian press report that the money was found in a luxurious Toronto apartment, while OCCRP placed the arrest itself at a strip mall. A later analysis at Cosa Nostra News dates the arrest to 8 August; the reports from the time say 7 August.

OCCRP reported that he was deported on the Tuesday and landed in Rome on Wednesday 20 August. Corriere reported that he came down at Rome's Ciampino airport at 6 a.m., escorted by ROS carabinieri and Canadian police, and was taken to a Rome prison.

Canada's public safety minister, Stockwell Day, thanked the Canada Border Services Agency for removing him quickly. In a 20 August statement he said it was "a great example of Canada's ability to coordinate efforts to combat transnational organized crime", adding that Canada "is not a safe haven for individuals who have gained admission to Canada by concealing their involvement in serious and organized crime."
An analyst writing on Gangsters Inc. says Coluccio then spent over four years under Italy's special "41-bis" prison regime.

His capture became part of a larger story within weeks. In September 2008, Italian and American authorities announced the results of Operation Solare, with arrests also made in Mexico and Guatemala. The BBC reported about 200 people held in four countries over alleged trans-Atlantic drug trafficking involving Mexico's Gulf cartel; US Attorney General Michael Mukasey called it a "massive assault" on the cartel and said the arrests followed a 15-month investigation. The BBC listed seizures of more than 16,000kg of cocaine, among other drugs, and about $60.1 million in US currency.

Corriere's English edition said that among the detained were sixteen members of the Aquino-Coluccio 'Ndrangheta gang from the Gioiosa Jonica area of Reggio Calabria province, picked up in New York and in Calabria. It said investigators had found the 'Ndrangheta's "well-established relations" in the United States and Canada, "where Giuseppe Coluccio was arrested in Toronto on 7 August". It also reported that on 22 May that year ROS inquiries allowed the seizure of 44 kilograms of cocaine posted from Venezuela and meant for the Aquino-Coluccio gang of Marina di Gioiosa Jonica. The reports do not charge Giuseppe Coluccio himself with the Solare shipments.

Salvatore Coluccio, wanted since 2005, was found on 10 May 2009 in his home in Marina di Gioiosa Ionica, according to Corriere and L'Unione Sarda. He was in a hiding place concealed behind a cavity that moved on a mechanical device, which had electricity, ventilation and food supplies. He was unarmed and did not resist. Carabinieri also burst into a hotel next to the house, owned by his in-laws, interrupting two wedding banquets. L'Unione Sarda described the two brothers as heads of the clan of the same name in the Gioiosa Ionica area.

Antonio, the last brother in Canada, fought for years to stay and left voluntarily in 2010 to avoid deportation, the National Post reported. The paper said he had been drawn into a large anti-mafia probe codenamed Operation Acero in 2015, and that in the week of its 19 July 2018 report a court convicted him and imposed 30 years plus a lifetime ban from public office, according to Italian media reports. The National Post wrote in 2013 that Giuseppe and Salvatore "were convicted for masterminding a vast, international drug trafficking network".

The clan's influence in Ontario outlasted his removal, according to Italian investigation material reported by an analyst on Gangsters Inc.. Carmine Verduci, whom that analyst describes as likely capo of the Toronto locale linked to Marina di Gioiosa Ionica, was shot dead on 24 April 2014 in the parking lot of a Woodbridge café. Italian investigators, quoted in the same article, suggested that the Figliomeni brothers had planned his killing after weapons disappeared, "with consequent responsibilities also ascribed to the boss Giuseppe Coluccio". The analyst says the killing was probably the result of a struggle for supremacy in Toronto's 'Ndrangheta, and that Italian interceptions told of Coluccio, by then out of prison, being ready to organise a retaliation using WhatsApp messages. The Moka Café shooting of 24 June 2015, which left two dead, is called by the analyst a probable retaliation; he adds that the gunman was convicted but that nobody has been traced as instigator. None of this was a finding against Giuseppe Coluccio, and the same article calls the retaliation link probable, not proven.

Italian magistrate Nicola Gratteri told the Globe and Mail in 2010 that Canada "is an important hideout, a place where many fugitives hide" and that Italian authorities had identified nine 'Ndrangheta clans in Ontario. The paper listed Coluccio's 2008 deportation, and the 2005 expulsion of Antonio Commisso, among cases in which fugitives were sent back from Canada. Canadian investigators pointed out to the paper that mere membership of a mafia group is a crime in Italy and is not one in Canada.
